ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A=80^\circ$. After cutting off $\angle A$, we obtain the quadrilateral $BCDE$. Then, what is the sum of $\angle 1 + \angle 2$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Given: $\because$ $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ are exterior angles of $\triangle ADE$,\\
$\therefore$ $\angle 1 = \angle ADE + \angle A$, $\angle 2 = \angle AED + \angle A$,\\
$\therefore$ $\angle 1 + \angle 2 = \angle ADE + \angle A + \angle AED + \angle A$,\\
Moreover, $\because$ $\angle ADE + \angle A + \angle AED = 180^\circ$,\\
$\therefore$ $\angle 1 + \angle 2 = 180^\circ + \angle A = \boxed{260^\circ}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a large triangle ABC, with vertex A above and B and C on the two sides at the bottom. Point E is on side AB, point D is on side AC, and line segment ED connects horizontally, cutting off the small triangle ADE at the top and forming quadrilateral BCDE below. The marked ∠1 is located at point E, below line segment ED, and is the exterior angle of the small triangle ADE at E; the marked ∠2 is located at point D, below line segment ED, and is the exterior angle of the small triangle ADE at D. The problem gives ∠A=80°. Reasoning: In triangle ADE, by the exterior angle theorem, the exterior angle ∠1 at E is equal to the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles, so ∠1=∠ADE+∠A. The exterior angle ∠2 at D is equal to the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles, so ∠2=∠AED+∠A. Adding the two equations gives ∠1+∠2=∠ADE+∠AED+2∠A. Also because the sum of the interior angles of triangle ADE is 180°, that is, ∠ADE+∠AED+∠A=180°, so ∠ADE+∠AED=180°-∠A. Therefore ∠1+∠2=(180°-∠A)+2∠A=180°+∠A=180°+80°=260°.
